replying_to: Replying to ASAP DML: Deep Metric Learning with Alternating Sets of Alternating Proxies
display_title: Official Review of Paper874 by Reviewer Ni5u

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an proxy-based approach to Deep Metric Learning which is formulated as a feasibility problem of finite chance constraints representing similarity and dissimilarty relations. The approach boils down to a standard regularized proxy-based objective which re-initializes multi proxies per class repeatedly over the course of training. Experiments show performance improvements using different DML loss functions.
content.main_review:
#### Strengths:
+ The paper is well written and presented.
+ The evaluation protocol considers the important benchmark sets for DML and also presents ablation studies to provide insights into the learning procedure and optimization.

#### Weaknesses:
- The presented formulation of (proxy-based) DML is very similar to the work [A], which also performs an optimization based on alternating projections onto feasible sets of constraints. While the presented approach embeds proxy-based learning into the optimization framework, [A] embeds sample-based learning. Although the optmization of the presented model is formulated using chance constraints, the core idea remains similar. Hence, theoretical significance is limited.

- The quantative evaluation lacks comparison to the recent state-of-the-art in Deep Metric Learning. Compared to [B,C,D,E] the presented model performs worse on all reported datasets (CUB200, CARS196, SOP, Inhop). Moreover, these models are based on a single model rather than forming an ensemble of 4 independent models, which achieves the best reported results (512D) in this paper. In particular the work of [B] is also proxy-based and therefore also conceptually similar. Hence, the presented model is inferior in performance to multiple previous works while requiring substantially more training time and resources, which reduces the empirical significance of the presented approach.

- Important state-of-the-art works in DML are not cited in the presented manuscript [B,D,E]. Moreover, also the approach [A] is not cited which is based on a very similar optimization formulation using projections onto feasible sets.

#### Questions:
- The results for dimensionality of 512 are based on an ensemble of 4 independent models. Why did you choose to use an ensemble to report results using 512d, instead of using an 512 dimensional embedding explicitly (single model) as it is the standard of the most recent works in DML? Showing the corresponding experiment (single model with 512d embedding layer) would be quite helpful for fair comparison to the state-of-the-art.
------------
References:

[A] Can et al. 2019; Deep Metric Learning with Alternating Projections onto Feasible Sets

[B] Gu et al. 2021; Proxy Synthesis: Learning with Synthetic Classes for Deep Metric Learning

[C] Milbich et al. 2020; DiVA: Diverse Visual Feature Aggregation for Deep Metric Learning

[D] Seidenschwarz et al 2021; Learning Intra-Batch Connections for Deep Metric Learning

[E] Roth et al. 2021; S2SD: Simultaneous Similarity-based Self-Distillation for Deep Metric Learning
content.summary_of_the_review: The presented work is conceptually similar to previous works and inferior in comparison to less complex and computationally more efficient state-of-the-art models (which are partly not mentioned in the manuscript). Hence, both theoretical and empirical significance justifying an acceptance is lacking.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ni5u (3/3)
content.comment:
### *[...Important state-of-the-art works in DML are not cited...]*

The mentioned methods [A, B, D, E] are very recent advances that are officially published no sooner that our work is completed. We will expand on our discussions in the related work to include those methods.

### *[...Why did you choose to use an ensemble to report results using 512d...]*

Recent works [1-3] show that **conventional evaluation** methods might **fail to reflect the unbiased improvement** of the methods. In fact, [1] shows **most of the claimed improvements are elaborated due to some flawed practices**. [1] proposes an evaluation procedure to compare the methods in many respects and benchmarks many well-accepted approaches. Recent works (e. g., [4, 5]) also follow [1]'s evaluation procedure. We also agree with the claims of [1] and **follow their evaluation method to provide unbiased contribution of our work** and to compare it with the other benchmarked approaches. We also discuss fairness of our evaluation procedure in the supplementary material.

**512D ensemble scores** are performance metrics proposed in [1] rather than an ensemble model. Averaged 128D score reflects how good the method's generalization is and 512D ensebmle score reflects how good the method's representation power is. We find evaluating the methods under the same settings with averaged and concatenated performances more technically sound. We can expand our supplementary material to include single model 512D results obtained with test data feedback.

[1] Musgrave, K., Belongie, S., & Lim, S. N. (2020, August). A metric learning reality check. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 681-699). Springer, Cham.

[2] Roth, K., Milbich, T., Sinha, S., Gupta, P., Ommer, B., & Cohen, J. P. (2020, November). Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 8242-8252). PMLR.

[3] Fehervari, I., Ravichandran, A., & Appalaraju, S. (2019). Unbiased evaluation of deep metric learning algorithms. arXiv preprint arXiv:1911.12528.

[4] Gu et al. 2021; Proxy Synthesis: Learning with Synthetic Classes for Deep Metric Learning

[5] Zhao, Wenliang, et al. "Towards Interpretable Deep Metric Learning with Structural Matching." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ni5u (2/3)
content.comment:
# The reviewer's claims are based on the factually incorrect interpretation of the experimental work and the related literature.

### *[...Compared to [B,C,D,E] the presented model performs worse on all reported datasets (CUB200, CARS196, SOP, Inhop)...]*

+ Among [B,C,D,E], **only [D] provides InShop results**. 

+ Among [B,C,D,E], **only [B]'s experimental setting matches ours**. Therefore, **directly comparing [C,D,E]'s results** with ours to assess superiority of the methods does **not technically sound**, as **claimed by independent works** [1-3]; since, they are **evaluated on different experimental settings**. Moreover, **only [B] provide MAP@R results** ([E]'s mAP@R formulation is actually P@R in our setting).

One **cannot factually conclude** that our method perform worse on **all four** (CUB200, CARS196, SOP, Inhop) datasets compared to [B,C,D,E].

### *[... these models are based on a single model...]*

**[B]'s 512D embeddings are concatenation of 128D embeddings of 4 independent models** as in our setting.

**[C] is a pseudo-ensemble method**: Learns **different embedding heads** for different tasks despite sharing the backbone.


### The reviewer's claim of *"[...the presented model is inferior in performance to multiple previous works..."]* is **factually not correct**.

+ **[B]'s best relative MAP@R improvements** over ProxyAnchor (best baseline in both) for CUB, CARS, and SOP are **0.67%, 0.34%, and 0.24%**, respectively; while **our MAP@R improvement** over ProxyAnchor for CUB, CARS and SOP are **0.91%, 1.41%, and 2.84%**, respectively (with MS loss owing to its ProxyAnchor loss relation).

+ **[B] achieves its best MAP@R** results with **28.11%, 29.71%, and 49.53%** in CUB, CAR and SOP, respectively; **we achieve** **28.02%, 29.14%, and 52.73%**. Performing **on par with [B] in CUB and CARS**, **our method is superior** with **at least 3% point margin** in **SOP**. Similarly, based on relative improvements, **our method is also superior in boosting the performance of the baseline methods**. Considering relative improvements over baselines are more meaningful due to slight Pytorch/Tensorflow  based performance differences.

---

+ **[C] achieves its best P@1** results with **66.8%, 84.1%, and 78.1%** in CUB, CAR, and SOP, respectively, for 512D embeddings trained with **batch size of 112** and **test data feedback**. **We achieve 69.73%, 86.26%, and 79.53%** with **batch size of 32** and **without test data feedback**.
---

+ **[D] uses ResNet50** which is known to be a **superior backbone** architecture **especially for large scale datasets** such as **SOP and InShop**. It **achieves 67.1%, 86.7%, 81.1% and, 92.5%** points **P@1** performance on CUB, CARS, SOP, and InShop, respectively. With inferior backbone (BN-Inception), **we achieve 69.73%, 86.26%, 79.53% and 90.24%** points **P@1** performance. We should note that P@1 is a noisy metric and can be boosted by sacrificing from MAP@R performance. Thus, **without [D]'s MAP@R results with BN-Inception**, we **cannot factually assess the superiority** of the two methods.

---

+ **[E] achieves its best P@1** results with **68.2%, 86.3%, and 78.9%** in CUB, CAR, and SOP, respectively, for 512D embeddings trained with **batch size of 112** and **test data feedback**. **We achieve 69.73%, 86.26%, and 79.53%** with **batch size of 32** and **without test data feedback**. Moreover, **[E]'s relative P@1 improvements** over MS are **2.5%, 2.2%, and 0.7%** points in CUB, CAR, and SOP, respectively. **Our relative P@1 improvements** over MS are **4.19%, 5.38%, and 6.84%**.

---

Besides the aforementioned facts, our empirical study includes SOTA loss terms, SOTA proxy-based approaches, and memory based XBM which is one of the best performing methods. We firmly believe that our empirical study covers enough comparisons to support the implications of our method as well as to show its superior performance.

### *[...while requiring substantially more training time and resources...]*

As we also discuss in our response to **R-a84G**, our method **marginally increase** the memory requirement (order of KBs in CUB, CAR, and MBs in SOP, InShop) and training time (10% increase). We also disclose the computation analysis in the supplementary material. Moreover, **[C] and [D] are more resource demanding** methods than ours.

------------------

[1] Musgrave, K., Belongie, S., & Lim, S. N. (2020, August). A metric learning reality check. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 681-699). Springer, Cham.

[2] Roth, K., Milbich, T., Sinha, S., Gupta, P., Ommer, B., & Cohen, J. P. (2020, November). Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 8242-8252). PMLR.

[3] Fehervari, I., Ravichandran, A., & Appalaraju, S. (2019). Unbiased evaluation of deep metric learning algorithms. arXiv preprint arXiv:1911.12528.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ni5u (1/3)
content.comment:
We thank **R-Ni5u** for their time and effort spent providing feedback. We address the specific concerns as follows:
 
### *[...The presented formulation of (proxy-based) DML is very similar to the work [A]...Hence, theoretical significance is limited...]*

As we also discuss in our response to **R-WF8a**, we firmly believe that **sharing similar ideas on the surface with [A] does not degrade the theoretical significance of our work** owing to the following reasons:

1. [A] is a **concurrent work** which had been under development and not been published by the time we were developing our method. **We approach the problem independently with a different perspective** that enables us to **formally** develop a method which **does not suffer from the many limitations that [A] does** (*please refer to our response to **R-WF8a**)*.
---------	

2. Our **starting point is very different** from [A]'s. We build on **chance-constrained problem** and develop our method upon **theoretical results**, which are supported by empirical studies as well. On the contrary, **[A] directly builds on training data based pairwise distance constraints similar to [1]** and come up with their method after **series of approximations without theoretical bounds**.
-----

3. Solving constrained problems with **alternating projections are not uncommon** in metric learning and **not the main contribution of our paper** either. In fact, **one of the pioneers** [1] involves **similar** alternating projections onto feasible sets to perform projected gradient ascent. **What makes our method unique is the theoretically sound way we connect the proxy and set intersection concepts to arbitrarily increase the number of class representatives exploited in the problem**.

In summary, **the core idea of our work is formulating DML as a chance-constrained problem**. Arriving at set intersection problem as well as alternating projections are just **the common practices we share with [A]**, which we believe, **does not make our contributions and especially theoretical significance of our paper limited**. If the core idea were that similar and our contributions were limited as **R-Ni5u** claimed, we would fail to come up with a theoretically and empirically superior method. 

--------------

[1] Xing, Eric, et al. "Distance metric learning with application to clustering with side-information." Advances in neural information processing systems 15 (2002): 521-528.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a proxy-based approach for deep metric learning by considering multiple proxies per class which reduces the covering radius and thus improving generalization performance. The method is evaluated on 4 bechmark DML datasets and achieves SOTA results.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 

1) Building on the current theories on the generalization bounds, the paper attempts to characterize and improve generalization bound for proxy-based DML. The reformulation of DML with chance constraint is interesting. 

2) The theory was supported with good experimental validation, specifically the ablation study and comparison with the baseline techniques. The proposed method achieves better performance compared to its baseline and also SOTA techniques.

Weaknesses:

1) One of the advantages of the proxy based methods is that they can generally convergence faster compared to pair based techniques. Since the paper also proposes a proxy-based technique, I would like to see the convergence speed of the proposed technique compared to another proxy-based techniques

2) Using more proxies/classes can lead to increase the total computational complexity of the proposed technique. I would like to see a comparison of the computational complexity of the proposed method with other proxy based techniques (not the timing info.). I see a marginal improvement on medium scale datasets like SOP. Increasing the computations to gain such marginal improvement may not be a good option.

3) One of the interesting applications of the metric learning problem is the scenarios where [Hyun Oh Song, 2016] there are huge number of classes and few samples in each class. Under these conditions, using multiple proxies (proposed technique) might not be helpful since one proxy can be close all the samples in the class. How can the proposed method be extended to such scenarios. I also noticed that the proposed technique significantly increases the cost (time required) for medium scale datasets like SOP. This shows the limitation of the technique for large scale datasets. I would like to see a discussion on this.

4) (Minor comment): The writing could be improved. It would be more readable if the authors move some of the equations to Appendix and explain the intuitions in the main text.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My rating is borderline. The paper proposes an interesting idea but I see that it works well on small datasets like CUB and CARS where there are more samples in a class (~100 samples/class) and hence using more proxies could help. But I would like to see a discussion about applying the proposed technique to datasets with large number of classes and few samples in each class. 
I would also like to see a comparison of the proposed technique with other proxy based methods on 1) convergence, 2) computational complexity.

content.title: Response to Reviewer a84G (2/2)
content.comment:
### *[...Using more proxies/classes can lead to increase the total computational complexity...]*

As we discuss in the supplementary material (A.3.3), using more proxies **marginally** increases ($\approx$ 5%-10%) computation during training. We **do not compute intra-proxy distance**; hence, the extra proxy-sample distance computations have marginal effect in GPU. Moreover, using more proxies **increases memory use only in the orders of KBs** (CUB, CARS) or **MBs** (SOP, InShop). The reviewer can refer to related section in the supplementary material for details.

**Inference has no additional computation nor memory** requirement.

### *[...I see a marginal improvement on medium scale datasets like SOP...]*

On the contrary, our improvements are **more significant in SOP and InShop** than CUB and CARS. We provide the related empirical results in Table-1 as well as summarized in Fig. 5 where ASAP-S denotes our method with 1-proxy per class, meaning that the same number of proxies is used as the proxy-based counter parts.

We have best relative improvements of $\approx$ **4% points MAP@R in CUB and Cars** whereas we have $\approx$ **10% points MAP@R in SOP and InSHOP**.

### *[...there are huge number of classes and few samples in each class...How can the proposed method be extended to such scenarios...]*

Our method **do not make any assumption on the number of samples** for each class. Therefore, our method **naturally extends** to such scenarios. In fact, our **SOP and InShop results empirically support such claim**. (SOP and InShop have 4-7 samples per class). 

Having small number of samples per class limits the representation power of the dataset, which is something we **cannot** control. 

### *[...using multiple proxies (proposed technique) might not be helpful since one proxy can be close all the samples in the class...]*

We should first note that **proposed method is not using multiple proxies**. We **do not have to have multiple-proxies** per class in each problem instance. Using 1 proxy per class, we can still arbitrarily increase the number of proxies exploited in the problem, as we show theoretically, which is the basis of our method.

If **one class proxy** happens to be **close enough to all the samples** in the corresponding class, then the embedding **problem is inherently solved**. With that being said, dataset samples do not constitute the whole set where the samples are drawn. To this end, DML approaches commonly employ data augmentation in practice to alleviate sparsity issue. Thus, using more proxies can still help for such scenarios as the empirical studies also show.

### *[...the proposed technique significantly increases the cost...]*

As we discuss in our aforementioned responses as well as in the supplementary material, we **do not significantly increase** the computation cost. **On the contrary, our method helps scalability**. Our proxy-based learning together with alternating projections **open a new direction** to consider more global information during mini-batch gradient updates. In this manner, our method brings significantly more performance improvements to the baseline losses in large scale datasets than in the smaller datasets like CUB and CARS.

content.title: Response to Reviewer a84G (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank **R-WF8a** for their positive feedback and acknowledgment of our contributions. We address the specific concerns as follows:

### *[...I would like to see the convergence speed of the proposed technique compared to another proxy-based techniques...]*

Our method does not necessarily enjoy relatively fast convergence of proxy-based methods; because, we exploit proxy-based learning for the intermediate problems rather than solving the main problem with a proxy-based loss. We **provide the optimization steps** per proxy-based problem instance **for several losses in Fig. 4(b)** from which relative convergence can be compared owing to each problem instance being a proxy-based method. Nevertheless, we also provide Table-1 below to compare the convergence of the methods for SOP and InShop datasets. The reported numbers are the rounded averages of the 4 models.

***Table-1: Optimization steps of training in SOP and InShop***

|    Method    | SOP | In-shop |
|:------------:|:-------:|:-------:|
|      C2      |  62K |   114K   |
|    C2-XBM    |  81K |    93K   |
|    C2-ASAP   |  69K |   127K   |
|      MS      |  67K |    98K   |
|    MS-ASAP   |  91K |   131K   |

We observe $\approx$ 10%-35% increase in the optimization steps for the pairwise losses.

### *[...I would like to see a comparison of the computational complexity of the proposed method with other proxy based techniques...]*

We have the same complexity in inference. During training, both the memory and computation marginally increase as we disclose in the supplementary material (A.3.3).

**SoftTriple uses more proxies** in CUB and CARS.

**XBM's memory size and our proxy number match** as we explain in the supplementary material (A.2-Hyperparameters-XBM).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper mainly targets deep metric learning. The authors solve the problem in three steps. They first reformulate the problem into a feasibility problem, then theoretical analysis is provided to show how increasing number of proxies can improve the generalization performance. After that a new algorithm including alternating projection and greedy proxy selection is proposed, which is assessed on several benchmark datasets.
content.main_review:
Pros:
1.	The methodology part is comprehensive. 
2.	This paper provides insightful explanation for proxy-based DML.

Problems:
1.	While the authors claim that the reformulation and the alternating projection are their contributions, these techniques have already been studied in DML [1]. I suggest the authors reclaim their contribution and discuss the relationship with this paper.
2.	The authors follow the protocol of [2] to conduct experiments. However most baseline results in Tab.1 are different from those in [2]. It would be better to explain the reason of difference.
3.	It is not clear why different ablation studies are conducted on different datasets, e.g. Fig.1 and Fig.2 are based on MNIST while Fig.3 and Fig.4 are based on CUB and Cars.
4.	It would be better to compare Fig.1 with a visualization without proxy selection, which according to the method should be the key to making use of multiple proxies.

[1] Can O, Gürbüz Y Z, Alatan A A. Deep Metric Learning With Alternating Projections Onto Feasible Sets[C]//2021 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP). IEEE, 2021: 1264-1268.
[2] Musgrave K, Belongie S, Lim S N. A metric learning reality check[C]//European Conference on Computer Vision. Springer, Cham, 2020: 681-699.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WF8a (2/2)
content.comment:
### 2) [*...most baseline results in Tab.1 are different from those in [2]...*]
The source of such discrepancy is twofold:

**1.** **Hyperparameters:** As we disclose in the supplementary material (A.2-Fairness, A.2-Hyperparameters), we consider the results of hyperparameter search in [2] together with the efforts of the original paper implementations to pick the best performing parameters for the baseline methods and compared methods. In some, the original works' hyperparameter settings exploit better potential of the corresponding methods. For those cases, our baseline performances are slightly higher than [2]'s; since, we use the original hyperparameter settings rather than [2]'s.

**2.** **ML-Library:** Pythorch library is used in [2]. We implemented our own framework in Tensorflow and evaluated all the compared methods in our framework to eliminate any framework related performance differences. It is well-known issue that methods have slight Pytorch and Tensorflow performance discrepancy owing to optimizer implementations. RMSProp with 1e-6 learning rate is used in [2]. However, based on our initial empirical studies, we find that Adam with 1e-5 learning rate performs better than RMSProp with 1e-6 learning rate. Though our baseline performances are slightly different, the relative performances of the methods are transferable to [2]'s.

### 3) [*...why different ablation studies are conducted on different datasets...*]

We should first note that **we use CUB**, **not MNIST**, in the empirical study summarized **in Fig. 2**.

***Proof of the concept tests (Fig. 1):*** We want to show the geometry of the embedding space in 2D without using dimension reduction for the sake of interpretability. Moreover, we want to show the effect of using proxies in place of class samples. For the latter, we need a dataset with small number of classes in order to contain class representatives in a batch together with the random samples. Thus, we use MNIST owing to its simplicity to be represented in 2D and few number of classes it has.

***Hyperparameter Search (Fig. 2):*** We use Bayesian search and it performs repetitive trainings. Among the four benchmark datasets, CUB has the smallest training duration. Therefore, we exploit CUB in Bayesian search for the sake of computational concerns.

***Ablation on Proxy Selection (Fig. 3 and Fig. 4):*** We mainly use CUB and CARS for this ablation study rather than SOP and InSop; since, SOP and InShop have relatively less number of samples for each class. For SOP and Inshop dataset, 7 samples per class cover almost the entire training set. Thus, we find it inconvenient to perform pool size ablation on those two, considering the computational load as well. Granted, we provide both random selection (no pool) and pool size of 7 samples per class in our quantitative results.

### 4-a) [*...which according to the method should be the key to making use of multiple proxies...*]

We should note that **the key** to making use of multiple proxies is **having diverse samples** to initialize the proxies. Random sampling indeed can provide diversity in the samples as well. Therefore, as long as we re-initialize the proxies with new samples, we will have some diverse proxies in multiple proxy case. With that being said, we use Greedy K-Center to pick the samples in a clever way to reduce the covering radius as much as we can (analogous to mining versus random sampling). **We provide the related comparisons in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4**, where proxy selection with *pool size = number of proxies* is equivalent to random sampling.

### 4-b) [*...a visualization without proxy selection...*]

We use Fig. 1 to concretely illustrate the effect of our method depicted in the corresponding schema. We defer the effect of the clever proxy selection over random sampling to Fig. 3 and Fig. 4.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WF8a (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank **R-WF8a** for their positive feedback and acknowledgment of our contributions. We address the specific concerns as follows:

### 1) [*...these techniques have already been studied in DML [1]...*]

Though, on the surface, our approach seems to share the ideas of set intersection and exploiting class representatives with the **concurrent work [1]**; we approach the problem **independently with a different perspective** that enables us to formally develop a method which does **not suffer from the poor scalability of exploiting class representatives as [1]'s method does**.

### Mainly, our works differs from [1] in that:

**1.** We provide **theoretically more solid foundation** to our method **with performance characterizations** whereas [1] implicitly **relies on zero-training error assumption** (Proposition 2.1) and **series of approximations without error bounds** to provide a practical algorithm.

In particular, [1] directly builds on the constraint set imposed by the training data and provides **no formal characterization** of such formulation on the generalization in the training domain.

We, on the other hand, **build on a single chance constraint to formulate the DML problem**, and by providing bounds for the approximation errors, we **formally show** that it can be decomposed into multiple chance constraints implied by proxy-based DML instances. We then consider **increasing the chance constraints through iterative projections** (*i. e.,* relating DML to set intersection problem).


**2.** One of the main claims of [1] is the benefit of exploiting particular samples repetitively in the consecutive batches (*i. e.,* class representatives). However, **for practical problems**, only a random subset of the class representatives can be included in the batches. Thus, the method **boils down to sampling from two different sets in large scale problems, deviating from the main claim**.

**We solve scalability problem** by formally relating proxy-based DML to solution of some chance constraints and further relating the intersection of such constraints sets to the solution of the DML problem.

In summary, [1] formulates DML as a set intersection problem to be solved by alternating projections and **shows that each projection instance is equivalent to a typical DML problem** after some approximations. **Differently**, we relate proxy-based DML to feasibility of some chance constrains and **use iterative projections to increase the number of chance constraints to be satisfied**.

We firmly believe that sharing similar spirits with [1] does not degrade the significance of our contributions. We should note that exploiting alternating projections is not one of the main contributions of our work. It is rather a common practice we use to solve set intersection problems. We should also note that the practice of using class representatives has been also discovered by many independent works. **What makes our method unique is the way we connect the two concepts to arbitrarily increase the number of class representatives exploited in the problem**.

We initially do not include [1] in our discussions; since, it had not been officially published at the time we were preparing our manuscript. With that being said, the method has been officially published rather recently and hence, we will expand on our discussions in the related work to include [1].
